title: EU NIS2 Directive Assessment
framing: A conformance and gap assessment against the cybersecurity risk-management and reporting obligations of the EU NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555), focused on governance (Article 20), the cybersecurity risk-management measures (Article 21(2)(a)-(j)) and incident-reporting obligations (Article 23). Each obligation is judged Achieved / Partially Achieved / Not Achieved by the consultant. This is a readiness and gap analysis to support improvement; it is not a determination of legal compliance with NIS2 or with the national law that transposes it in any given Member State.
sourceNote: Items are paraphrased from the Articles of Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2). Article and clause references are given per item. NIS2 is transposed into national law by each Member State, which may add or detail requirements; confirm scope against the applicable national transposition. Verify the paraphrased wording against the official Official Journal text before relying on it. Version-stamp when finalised. The 'rationale' (why this matters) given for each obligation is best-practice interpretation drawing on recognised frameworks (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, ENISA guidance) to explain the security intent; it is not text from, or a legal interpretation of, the Directive.

categories.name: Risk analysis and information system security policies
Security in acquisition, development and maintenance
HR security, access control and asset management

items.title: Management approval of measures
items.requirement: The management body approves the cybersecurity risk-management measures taken by the entity to comply with Article 21.
items.rationale: Senior approval turns cybersecurity from an IT issue into a governed business risk: it gives the measures the mandate, funding and authority to be enforced, and ensures someone owns the residual risk. NIS2 places this responsibility explicitly on management.
items.evidencePrompt: Record evidence of management-body approval (minutes, sign-off) and the basis for the state selected.

items.title: Oversight of implementation
items.requirement: The management body oversees the implementation of the cybersecurity risk-management measures.
items.rationale: Approval without oversight lets controls decay. Regular management review of progress, KPIs and exceptions keeps the programme on track and surfaces slippage before it becomes an incident.
items.evidencePrompt: Record how management oversees implementation (reporting, reviews, KPIs).

items.title: Management accountability
items.requirement: Accountability of the management body for compliance with the cybersecurity risk-management measures is established and understood.
items.rationale: Clear, understood accountability at board level sets the tone from the top and ensures security decisions are owned rather than diffused. It is increasingly what regulators and insurers expect to see evidenced.
items.evidencePrompt: Record how accountability is assigned and understood at management level.

items.title: Management training
items.requirement: Members of the management body follow training to gain sufficient knowledge and skills to identify risks and assess cybersecurity risk-management practices and their impact on the entity.
items.rationale: A board cannot oversee a risk it does not understand. Management training builds the literacy needed to challenge assumptions, prioritise investment and judge whether the measures are proportionate to the threat.
items.evidencePrompt: Record management training undertaken and its scope.

items.title: Staff training offered
items.requirement: The entity offers similar cybersecurity training to its employees on a regular basis.
items.rationale: People are the most frequently exploited attack surface. Regular, role-relevant training measurably reduces susceptibility to phishing and social engineering and reinforces a security-aware culture.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the staff training programme, cadence and coverage.

items.title: Risk analysis policy
items.requirement: Policies on risk analysis are in place, based on an all-hazards approach to protecting network and information systems and their physical environment.
items.rationale: Risk-based prioritisation is the foundation of every credible security programme. An all-hazards risk analysis directs effort and spend at the threats that matter most, rather than spreading them thinly or chasing the latest headline.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the risk analysis policy/methodology and how risks are identified and treated.

items.title: Information system security policy
items.requirement: An information system security policy is established, approved by management, and communicated.
items.rationale: A management-approved, communicated security policy sets the expected baseline and the authority behind it. Without one, controls are applied inconsistently and staff have no clear standard to follow.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the security policy, its approval and how it is communicated and maintained.

items.title: Incident handling capability
items.requirement: An incident handling capability covering detection, analysis, containment, response and recovery is in place.
items.rationale: Serious incidents are a matter of when, not if. A defined detect-analyse-contain-respond-recover capability limits dwell time and impact; ad-hoc response typically multiplies the damage, cost and recovery time.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the incident handling process, roles and tooling.

items.title: Incident logging and lessons learned
items.requirement: Incidents are logged and post-incident review feeds improvements to controls and the response capability.
items.rationale: Logging and post-incident review turn incidents into improvement. Without that feedback loop the same root causes recur and the organisation never matures its defences.
items.evidencePrompt: Record incident records and examples of lessons-learned changes.

items.title: Backup management
items.requirement: Backups of critical systems and data are taken, protected and tested for restoration.
items.rationale: Tested, protected (offline or immutable) backups are the single most effective control against ransomware and destructive attacks. Untested or online-only backups routinely fail exactly when they are needed.
items.evidencePrompt: Record backup scope, protection (offline/immutable) and last restoration test.

items.title: Disaster recovery
items.requirement: Disaster recovery plans exist for critical systems and services, with defined recovery objectives.
items.rationale: Defined recovery objectives and tested DR plans decide whether a major outage is an inconvenience or an existential event. Recovery time and point objectives must be known and proven, not assumed.
items.evidencePrompt: Record DR plans, recovery objectives and test history.

items.title: Crisis management
items.requirement: Crisis management arrangements (roles, decision-making and communications) are defined and exercised.
items.rationale: Technical recovery is only half of a crisis. Pre-agreed roles, decision rights and communications prevent paralysis and reputational damage when senior, legal and external stakeholders must act under pressure.
items.evidencePrompt: Record crisis management arrangements and exercises.

items.title: Supplier risk management
items.requirement: Security risks arising from relationships with direct suppliers and service providers are assessed and addressed.
items.rationale: Attackers increasingly enter through trusted third parties. Assessing supplier and service-provider risk closes a blind spot that perimeter controls cannot, and is central to NIS2's emphasis on supply-chain security.
items.evidencePrompt: Record supplier risk assessments and how risks are addressed in relationships and contracts.

items.title: Supplier security requirements
items.requirement: Security requirements are set for suppliers, including the security of products and services, and adherence is monitored.
items.rationale: Security expectations that are not contracted and monitored are not enforceable. Setting and checking supplier requirements ensures third parties uphold the same baseline and that product and service security is maintained over time.
items.evidencePrompt: Record supplier security requirements and monitoring of adherence.

items.title: Secure acquisition, development and maintenance
items.requirement: Security is addressed in the acquisition, development and maintenance of network and information systems.
items.rationale: Building and buying securely is far cheaper than retrofitting. Addressing security across acquisition, development and maintenance prevents weaknesses being designed in and carried through the system lifecycle.
items.evidencePrompt: Record secure development/acquisition practices and maintenance controls.

items.title: Vulnerability handling and disclosure
items.requirement: Vulnerabilities are identified, triaged and remediated, and there is a route for vulnerability disclosure.
items.rationale: Most breaches exploit known, unpatched vulnerabilities. A managed identify-triage-remediate process, plus a disclosure route, shrinks the window of exposure that attackers depend on.
items.evidencePrompt: Record vulnerability management process and disclosure handling.

items.title: Effectiveness assessment
items.requirement: Policies and procedures are in place to assess the effectiveness of the cybersecurity risk-management measures.
items.rationale: Controls that are never tested give false assurance. Assessment, testing and metrics confirm that measures work as intended and provide the evidence needed for governance and continual improvement.
items.evidencePrompt: Record how the effectiveness of measures is assessed (audits, testing, metrics).

items.title: Basic cyber hygiene
items.requirement: Basic cyber hygiene practices are defined and applied (e.g. updates, configuration, least privilege, awareness).
items.rationale: A large share of attacks are stopped by fundamentals: patching, secure configuration, least privilege and awareness. A defined hygiene baseline removes the easy wins attackers rely on.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the cyber hygiene baseline and how it is applied.

items.title: Cybersecurity training
items.requirement: Cybersecurity training is provided to relevant staff.
items.rationale: Sustained, relevant training keeps the human layer resilient as threats evolve. One-off awareness fades; regular reinforcement is what actually changes behaviour.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the training programme and coverage.

items.title: Cryptography and encryption
items.requirement: Policies and procedures on the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption are in place.
items.rationale: Encryption protects confidentiality and integrity when other controls fail: in transit, at rest and on lost devices. A clear policy ensures it is applied consistently and with sound key management rather than piecemeal.
items.evidencePrompt: Record cryptography/encryption policy and where encryption is applied.

items.title: Human resources security
items.requirement: Human resources security measures are in place (e.g. screening where lawful, terms of employment, joiners/movers/leavers).
items.rationale: Risk follows people through the employment lifecycle. Screening where lawful, clear terms and disciplined joiners/movers/leavers processes prevent orphaned accounts and reduce insider exposure.
items.evidencePrompt: Record HR security measures across the employment lifecycle.

items.title: Access control
items.requirement: Access control policies manage identities and privileges and enforce least privilege.
items.rationale: Least-privilege access control limits how far an attacker or a mistake can spread. Unmanaged identities and excess privilege are among the most common enablers of serious breaches.
items.evidencePrompt: Record access control policy, identity lifecycle and least-privilege enforcement.

items.title: Asset management
items.requirement: Assets are identified, classified and managed throughout their lifecycle.
items.rationale: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. A maintained, classified asset inventory underpins patching, monitoring, access control and incident response; gaps in it become unmonitored entry points.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the asset inventory, classification and management process.

items.title: Multi-factor authentication
items.requirement: Multi-factor or continuous authentication solutions are used where appropriate, in particular for remote and privileged access.
items.rationale: Passwords alone are routinely phished or stolen. MFA (especially for remote and privileged access) blocks the overwhelming majority of account-takeover attacks and is among the highest-value controls available.
items.evidencePrompt: Record where MFA/continuous authentication is enforced and any gaps.

items.title: Secured communications
items.requirement: Secured voice, video and text communications and secured emergency communication systems are used within the entity, where appropriate.
items.rationale: Secured and resilient communications protect sensitive exchanges from interception and keep the organisation able to coordinate during an incident, when normal channels may themselves be compromised.
items.evidencePrompt: Record secured and emergency communications arrangements.

items.title: Significant-incident identification
items.requirement: The entity can identify significant incidents against the Article 23 criteria (significant operational disruption or financial loss, or impact on others through considerable material or non-material damage).
items.rationale: If an entity cannot recognise a significant incident against the criteria, every downstream reporting deadline is missed by default. Correct, timely identification is the trigger for the entire reporting obligation.
items.evidencePrompt: Record how significant incidents are identified and the criteria used.

items.title: Early warning (24 hours)
items.requirement: A process exists to submit an early warning to the CSIRT or competent authority without undue delay and within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident.
items.rationale: The 24-hour early warning is a hard regulatory deadline. A rehearsed process and known contact routes are essential, because 24 hours is far too short to improvise under incident pressure.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the early-warning process and contact routes.

items.title: Incident notification (72 hours)
items.requirement: A process exists to submit an incident notification within 72 hours, updating the early warning with an initial assessment of the incident, its severity and impact, and indicators of compromise where available.
items.rationale: The 72-hour notification commits the entity to an initial severity and impact assessment. Pre-defined content and clear ownership ensure a timely, credible submission rather than a scramble.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the 72-hour notification process and content.

items.title: Final report (one month)
items.requirement: A process exists to submit a final report within one month, with a detailed description, severity and impact, root cause, mitigations applied, and any cross-border impact.
items.rationale: The one-month final report demonstrates root-cause understanding and effective mitigation to the authority. A defined process ensures the analysis is complete and defensible rather than retrofitted.
items.evidencePrompt: Record the final-report process and content.

items.title: Recipient notification
items.requirement: Where appropriate, recipients of the entity's services are notified of significant incidents and of any measures or remedies they can take in response.
items.rationale: Promptly informing affected service recipients (and telling them what they can do) limits downstream harm and protects trust, and may be required where the incident affects the services they rely on.
items.evidencePrompt: Record how and when service recipients are notified.

_contentNote: Categories follow NIS2 Article 20 (governance), Article 21(2)(a)-(j) (the ten risk-management measures) and Article 23 (reporting). Items paraphrase the obligations into assessable statements; they are not verbatim Directive text. Confirm against the official Official Journal text and the relevant national transposition.
seriesContext: The NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 is European law. It does not apply directly: each member state transposes it into national law, so the obligations an entity actually faces are set nationally and can differ between states, as can the supervisory regime and penalties. This assessment reads the Directive's own obligations. It is a gap analysis to support preparation, not a legal opinion and not a determination by a competent authority.
